lead: You can solve a linear system without ever touching the unknowns, by pushing the augmented matrix into a staircase shape. Three reversible row moves change how the matrix looks but not which values of x, y, z satisfy it. Repeat the moves and the equations practically solve themselves: the last row gives one unknown, then you work upward. Every solver you use — a calculator, a Python call, an exam answer — runs on these moves, and the staircase form is also the natural first step in later work on rank, on LU factorization and on determinants.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for the augmented matrix [A | b] and for what counts as a solution of a linear system.

blocks.text: Each row of an augmented matrix is one equation. An elementary row operation changes the matrix but must leave the solution set exactly as it was. Three moves pass that test.
Swap Ri ↔ Rj: exchange two rows. Undo it by swapping the same two rows back.
Scale kRi: multiply every entry of row i by a nonzero number k. Undo it by (1/k)Ri. The condition k ≠ 0 matters: 0·Ri wipes an equation out and no move brings it back.
Add a multiple Ri + kRj: replace row i by itself plus k times row j, with i ≠ j. Undo it by Ri − kRj. Here k = 0 is allowed but useless — nothing changes.

Each move is reversible, and its reverse is again one of the three. So the solution set stays fixed at every step: any solution of the old system satisfies the new rows, and reversing the step gives the old rows back. Two matrices joined by a chain of elementary row operations are row equivalent, written A ~ B.
Apply each move to the whole row, augmented column included. Those last-column numbers are part of each equation, and leaving them behind is the single most common arithmetic slip in an exam.
These moves are the engine of the unit: Chapter 1.3 strings them into an algorithm, and Chapter 1.5 stores the multipliers as a matrix.

sections.h3: Pivot, echelon form, reduced echelon form

blocks.text: The pivot (also called the leading entry) of a row is its first nonzero entry, counting from the left. A row of all zeros has no pivot.
Row echelon form (REF) is a staircase. A matrix is in echelon form when:

items: every nonzero row lies above every zero row;
each pivot is strictly to the right of the pivot in the row above;
every entry below a pivot is 0.

blocks.text: The pivots step down and to the right. Entries above a pivot and to its right may be anything at all.

Reduced row echelon form (RREF) keeps that staircase and cleans it further: every pivot equals 1, and every pivot is the only nonzero entry in its column, so zeros stand above it as well as below. Some syllabi call RREF the row canonical form or the fully reduced normal form.

Echelon form is not unique: two students can stop at different valid staircases for the same matrix and both be right. RREF is unique — a matrix has exactly one reduced form, whatever legal order of moves you choose. That is why a checked answer is quoted in RREF.

items: Start at the top row. Find the leftmost column that still has a nonzero entry at or below the current row; if that entry sits lower down, swap it up. It becomes the new pivot.
Clear below: for each row under the pivot, apply R<sub>i</sub> + kR<sub>j</sub> so the pivot column entry becomes 0.
Move one row down and one column right, and repeat until rows or columns run out. You now hold an echelon form.
To reach RREF, work upward: scale each pivot row so its pivot becomes 1, then clear the entries above each pivot with R<sub>i</sub> + kR<sub>j</sub>.

blocks.where: row p holds the pivot a<sub>pc</sub> in pivot column c; a<sub>ic</sub> is the entry being cleared in row i; k is the multiplier that makes the new entry in column c equal 0.

blocks.text: Scaling a pivot row to 1 first keeps the arithmetic in small numbers; many examiners accept either order. The flow chart below shows the two passes, downward then upward, from the augmented matrix to the unique reduced form. Worked counts for a longer system are in Chapter 1.3.

spec.aria: A top-to-bottom flow from the augmented matrix through pivot choice and clearing below to echelon form, then clearing above to the reduced form.

examples.question: Solve the system x + 2y + z = 4, 2x + 5y + 3z = 9, x + 3y + 3z = 6 by reducing its augmented matrix to echelon form, then to reduced row echelon form.
steps: Pivot is 1 in row 1, column 1. R₂ − 2R₁ gives [2−2, 5−4, 3−2, 9−8] = [0, 1, 1, 1].
Pivot is 1 in row 2, column 2. R₃ − R₂ gives [0, 1−1, 2−1, 2−1] = [0, 0, 1, 1].
Echelon form: [[1, 2, 1, 4], [0, 1, 1, 1], [0, 0, 1, 1]]. The last row reads z = 1.
Clear above the pivot in column 3: R₂ − R₃ gives [0, 1, 0, 0], so y = 0.
R₁ − R₃ gives [1, 2, 0, 3]. R₁ − 2R₂ gives [1, 0, 0, 3], so x = 3.
Check in the original equations: 3 + 0 + 1 = 4; 6 + 0 + 3 = 9; 3 + 0 + 3 = 6. All three hold.
examples.check:
from fractions import Fraction as F
M = [[F(1),F(2),F(1),F(4)],
     [F(2),F(5),F(3),F(9)],
     [F(1),F(3),F(3),F(6)]]
n = 3
for c in range(n):
    p = next(r for r in range(c, n) if M[r][c] != 0)
    M[c], M[p] = M[p], M[c]
    for r in range(n):
        if r != c and M[r][c] != 0:
            f = M[r][c] / M[c][c]
            M[r] = [M[r][k] - f*M[c][k] for k in range(n+1)]
for i in range(n):
    print(int(M[i][n] / M[i][i]))

traps: Multiplying a row by 0 to 'clear' it. Only k ≠ 0 is legal in kR<sub>i</sub>; a zeroed row cannot be recovered and the solution set is destroyed.
Forgetting the augmented column. R₂ − 2R₁ must be applied to the entry in [A | b] too, not only to the coefficient columns.
Believing echelon form is unique. Two different correct staircases of the same matrix are both right; finish both to RREF before deciding anything is wrong.
Writing 2R₁ − R₂ where the needed step is R₂ − 2R₁. The first form rescales row 1 and moves the pivot; the second keeps row 1 untouched.
Leaving a zero row between two nonzero rows. Echelon form demands every zero row sit at the bottom.

quiz.q: State the three elementary row operations and, for each, the operation that reverses it.
quiz.a: Swap R<sub>i</sub> ↔ R<sub>j</sub>, reversed by R<sub>i</sub> ↔ R<sub>j</sub>. Scale kR<sub>i</sub> with k ≠ 0, reversed by (1/k)R<sub>i</sub>. Add R<sub>i</sub> + kR<sub>j</sub> with i ≠ j, reversed by R<sub>i</sub> − kR<sub>j</sub>.

quiz.q: Why is k = 0 banned in kR<sub>i</sub> but harmless in R<sub>i</sub> + kR<sub>j</sub>?
quiz.a: Scaling by 0 turns the row into zeros and loses an equation that no legal move can rebuild. Adding 0 times another row changes nothing, so the move is still reversible — it is its own reverse.

quiz.q: Carry the same matrix A to reduced row echelon form.
A student reduces one matrix to two different echelon forms. Must at least one be wrong?
quiz.a: No. Echelon form is not unique, and different orders of legal moves give different staircases. Test by finishing both to RREF: RREF is unique, so both must reach the same matrix.

quiz.q: Explain why every elementary row operation preserves the solution set, and hence why row-equivalent matrices have the same solutions.
quiz.a: Each operation is undone by another operation of the same type. So every solution of the original system satisfies the new rows, and the reverse step shows every solution of the new system satisfies the original rows. The two solution sets are equal, and a chain of such steps carries the equality along.

quiz.q: Why must each pivot be scaled to 1 in RREF but not in echelon form?
quiz.a: Forcing pivots to 1 removes the freedom left by scaling, so only one reduced matrix can result and the answer can be read off directly. Echelon form allows any nonzero pivot.

beyond: Not for the exam. RREF is a canonical form: every matrix in a row-equivalence class has exactly one, which is why computer algebra systems can compare two matrices for row equivalence by comparing RREFs. Over exact arithmetic the reduction is done with fractions or with fraction-free variants such as the Bareiss algorithm, which keeps entries integral. In floating point, the choice of pivot becomes a numerical question — partial pivoting picks the largest available entry to limit rounding error — and this is what library solvers actually do. Search 'partial pivoting', 'Bareiss algorithm' or 'reduced row echelon form uniqueness proof' to go further.
